## Section 302 IPC / Section 101 BNS 2023 — MURDER

**Definition:** Culpable homicide is murder when the act is done with intention of causing death, or with knowledge that the act is so imminently dangerous it will in all probability cause death.

**Ingredients to establish:**
1. Death of a human being
2. Caused by the accused's act
3. The act was done with the intention to cause death (S.300 IPC), OR with knowledge that the act is likely to cause death

**Punishment:** Death OR Imprisonment for Life + Fine (no minimum — court decides based on facts)

**Procedural facts:**
- Offence: Cognizable, Non-bailable, Non-compoundable
- Triable by: Sessions Court exclusively
- Investigation: Police can arrest without warrant

**Death Penalty — 'Rarest of Rare' Doctrine:**
- Established in *Bachan Singh v State of Punjab (AIR 1980 SC 898)*
- Confirmed in *Macchi Singh v State of Punjab (1983)*
- Courts must consider aggravating vs. mitigating circumstances
- Factors: manner of killing, motive, social impact, criminal background of accused

**Distinction: Murder vs. Culpable Homicide (S.304 IPC)**
| Feature | Murder (S.302) | Culpable Homicide (S.304) |
|---|---|---|
| Intention | To cause death | May or may not intend death |
| Knowledge | Knows act will cause death | Knows act may cause death |
| Punishment | Death / Life | Up to 10 yrs / Life |

**BNS 2023 Update:** Section 101 retains the same definition and punishment. Trial now governed by BNSS 2023 instead of CrPC.

**Key case laws:**
- *Bachan Singh v State of Punjab* — Rarest of rare doctrine
- *State of UP v Satish* (2005 SC) — Life imprisonment norm; death sentence exception
- *Lehna v State of Haryana* — Mental health as mitigating factor

## Section 304 IPC / Section 105 BNS — Culpable Homicide Not Amounting to Murder

**When culpable homicide is NOT murder (exceptions to S.300):**
1. Act done in sudden and grave provocation (Exception 1)
2. Exceeding right of private defence (Exception 2)
3. Public servant exceeding powers (Exception 3)
4. Sudden fight without premeditation (Exception 4)
5. Consent of the deceased (Exception 5)

**Part I:** Where the act is done with intention of causing death — RI for Life OR up to 10 years + Fine
**Part II:** Where done with knowledge only — up to 10 years OR fine OR both

**Landmark cases:**
- *State of AP v R. Punnayya* — Distinction between S.299 and S.300 explained
- *K.M. Nanavati v State of Maharashtra* — Grave and sudden provocation discussed
pun: Part I: Life/10 yrs + Fine; Part II: 10 yrs/Fine or both

## Section 307 IPC / Section 109 BNS 2023 — Attempt to Murder

**Essential ingredients:**
1. The act must be done with such intention/knowledge that if death resulted, it would be murder
2. The accused must have done some act towards commission of murder
3. Actual death need not result

**Punishment:**
- If no hurt caused: Up to 10 years + Fine
- If hurt caused: Life imprisonment OR up to 10 years + Fine
- If already serving life sentence and causes hurt: Death or enhanced punishment

**Key distinction from S.302:** Attempt is punished even when death does not result, provided the intention/knowledge to murder existed.

**Case laws:**
- *State of Maharashtra v Balram Bama Patil* — Intention at the time of act is crucial
- *Om Prakash v State of Punjab* — Acts preparatory vs. acts in furtherance of attempt
pun: Up to 10 yrs + Fine; Life imprisonment if hurt caused

## Section 376 IPC / Section 63 BNS 2023 / POCSO Act — Rape & Sexual Offences

**Definition (S.375 IPC / S.63 BNS):** Non-consensual sexual intercourse with a woman. Includes seven categories of acts without consent.

**Punishment under S.376 IPC:**
- Basic: Minimum 10 years RI, may extend to imprisonment for life (natural life) + Fine
- Gang Rape (S.376D): Minimum 20 years to life imprisonment + Fine
- Rape on woman under 12 yrs (S.376AB): Minimum 20 yrs to life or death + Fine
- Rape on woman under 16 yrs (S.376(3)): Minimum 20 yrs to life + Fine

**Procedural safeguards:**
- Trial must be conducted in-camera (S.327 CrPC)
- Victim identity shall NOT be disclosed (S.228A IPC / S.73 BNSS)
- Complainant examined only by woman police officer
- Medical examination within 24 hours
- Investigation to be completed within 2 months (S.173(1A) CrPC)

**Consent (S.90 IPC):** Consent obtained by fear, misconception of fact, or from unsound mind is NOT valid consent.

**POCSO Act 2012 (Protection of Children from Sexual Offences):**
- Applies when victim is below 18 years
- Penetrative sexual assault (S.3): Minimum 10 years to life + Fine
- Aggravated penetrative sexual assault (S.5): Minimum 20 years to life/death + Fine
- Designated Special Courts for POCSO trials
- Presumption of guilt on accused in certain cases (S.29 POCSO)

**BNS 2023:** S.63 retains same definition; S.70 covers gang rape.

**Key cases:**
- *Tukaram v State of Maharashtra (Mathura Case)* — led to 1983 rape law amendments
- *Delhi Gang Rape Case (State v Ram Singh)* — led to 2013 Criminal Law Amendment
- *Independent Thought v UOI* (2017 SC) — marital rape of minor wife criminalised
pun: Min 10 yrs RI, up to Life (natural) + Fine. Gang rape: Min 20 yrs to Life

## Section 420 IPC / Section 318 BNS 2023 — Cheating

**Essentials (all four must be proven):**
1. **Deception** of the victim by the accused
2. Victim was **induced** by such deception
3. Victim **delivered property** or consented to modification/destruction of property
4. Accused had **dishonest intention at the time of deception** (not after)

**Ingredients checklist:**
- Accused made a representation
- Representation was false (accused knew this)
- Victim believed the false representation
- Victim acted upon it and delivered property/suffered loss
- Accused dishonestly received the benefit

**Punishment:** Up to 7 years imprisonment + Fine

**Related offences:**
- S.415 IPC: Cheating (basic definition) — covers both property delivery and inducement to do/omit acts
- S.417 IPC: Punishment for basic cheating — up to 1 year or fine or both
- S.418 IPC: Cheating with knowledge that wrongful loss will result
- S.419 IPC: Cheating by personation — up to 3 years

**Key principle — Mens rea:** Dishonest intention must exist at the INCEPTION of the transaction. If intent develops later, it may be breach of contract, not cheating.

**Case laws:**
- *Vesa Holdings v State of Kerala (2015)* — Dishonest intention from the beginning is essential element
- *Hridaya Ranjan Prasad v State of Bihar* — Promise not kept does not automatically mean cheating; dishonest intent must be proved
- *Dr. S. Dutt v State of UP* — Mere failure to pay back loan ≠ cheating

## Section 498A IPC / Section 85 BNS 2023 — Cruelty by Husband/Relatives

**Cruelty is defined as:**
1. **Physical/mental harassment** causing grave injury or danger to life, limb, or health of the woman, OR
2. **Harassment for unlawful demands** — coercing her or her relatives to meet demands for property/dowry

**Who can be charged:** Husband AND relatives of the husband (parents-in-law, siblings, etc.)

**Punishment:** Up to 3 years imprisonment + Fine

**Critical SC Guidelines — Arnesh Kumar v State of Bihar (2014):**
- Police CANNOT make automatic arrests under S.498A
- Magistrate must apply mind before granting remand
- Police must satisfy checklist (S.41 CrPC) before arrest
- Failure to follow = contempt of court

**Complaint procedure:**
- FIR can be filed by wife herself or a relative
- Filed at nearest police station or online (Mahila Thana)
- Women's Helpline: 181 | Police: 100

**Important points:**
- BOTH S.498A (criminal) and PWDVA 2005 (civil/criminal) can be filed simultaneously
- S.498A is non-bailable but magistrate can grant bail
- Frequently combined with S.304B (dowry death) charge

**Frequently cited cases:**
- *Arnesh Kumar v State of Bihar (2014)* — mandatory guidelines for arrest
- *Sushil Kumar Sharma v UOI* — S.498A does not violate constitutional rights

## Section 304B IPC / Section 80 BNS 2023 — Dowry Death

**All five elements must be proved:**
1. Death of a woman by burns OR bodily injury OR under suspicious circumstances
2. Death occurred within **7 years of marriage**
3. Before her death she was subjected to cruelty or harassment
4. Such cruelty/harassment was by husband or his relatives
5. Such cruelty/harassment was in connection with demand for **dowry**

**Punishment:** Minimum **7 years** RI, may extend to Life imprisonment

**Statutory Presumption — S.113B Indian Evidence Act:**
Once the prosecution proves the five ingredients above, the court SHALL presume that the husband or his relatives caused the dowry death. **Burden of proof SHIFTS to accused** to rebut this presumption.

**Frequently charged alongside:**
- S.498A IPC (cruelty)
- S.302 IPC (murder, if direct evidence available)
- Dowry Prohibition Act 1961 (for dowry demand itself)

**Definition of 'Dowry':** Dowry Prohibition Act — any property or valuable security given or agreed to be given in connection with marriage.

**Key cases:**
- *State of Punjab v Iqbal Singh* — Seven-year rule is strict; cannot extend beyond it
- *Hem Chand v State of Haryana* — Demand for dowry need not be expressed; can be inferred from circumstances
- *Rajbir v State of Haryana* — S.304B and S.302 can be charged simultaneously if evidence permits
pun: Minimum 7 years RI, may extend to Life

## Section 438 CrPC / Section 482 BNSS 2023 — Anticipatory Bail

**What it is:** A direction to release a person on bail in anticipation of arrest — even before arrest is made. Applied when a person has reason to believe they may be arrested for a non-bailable offence.

**Where to apply:** Sessions Court OR High Court (concurrent jurisdiction)

**Factors courts consider (S.438(1) CrPC):**
1. Nature and gravity of the accusation
2. Antecedents of the applicant (prior criminal record)
3. Possibility of applicant fleeing from justice
4. Whether accusation is made to humiliate/injure the applicant

**Conditions that can be attached (S.438(2)):**
- Making available for interrogation as required
- Not leaving India without court permission
- Not influencing witnesses
- Surrendering passport
- Any other condition the court deems fit

**Duration:** After *Sushila Aggarwal v State (NCT of Delhi) (2020 SC)* — anticipatory bail can continue till end of trial unless special reasons exist to limit its period.

**Important distinctions:**
| Feature | Regular Bail (S.437) | Anticipatory Bail (S.438) |
|---|---|---|
| Timing | After arrest | Before arrest |
| Who applies | Arrested person | Person apprehending arrest |
| Court | Any Magistrate | Sessions Court / HC |
| Effect | Release from custody | Protects from arrest |

**Key cases:**
- *Gurbaksh Singh Sibbia v State of Punjab (1980 SC)* — Seminal judgment; liberal approach
- *Sushila Aggarwal v State (2020 SC)* — Anticipatory bail can cover entire trial
- *HDFC Bank v J.J. Mannan* — Conditions for AB in economic offences

## Section 84 IPC — Insanity / Unsoundness of Mind as Defence

**Complete defence when established:** Nothing is an offence done by a person who, at the time of committing it, by reason of unsoundness of mind, is incapable of knowing the nature of the act, OR knowing that the act is wrong or contrary to law.

**McNaughton Rules (adopted by Indian courts):**
1. The accused was suffering from mental illness at the time of the act
2. As a result, they could not understand the nature and quality of the act, OR
3. Did not know what they were doing was wrong

**Burden of proof:** On the accused — balance of probabilities (S.105 Indian Evidence Act).

**Key distinctions:**
- S.84 requires TOTAL unsoundness — partial insanity insufficient
- Insanity must exist AT THE TIME of the offence (not before/after)
- Lucid intervals: If act done during lucid interval, S.84 does not apply
- Intoxication by others' agency (S.85 IPC): Full defence possible

**Case laws:**
- *Surendra Mishra v State of Jharkhand (2011)* — Mere abnormality of mind does not attract S.84
- *State of MP v Ahmadullah (1961)* — Clear proof of insanity at time of offence required
pun: If defence succeeds — acquittal / detention under mental health law

## Sections 96–106 IPC / Sections 34–44 BNS — Right of Private Defence

**Nature of the right:** Every person has the right to defend their own body and property, and the body and property of others, against any offence.

**Right of private defence of BODY (S.97/100 IPC) extends to causing DEATH when:**
1. Assault causing reasonable apprehension of death
2. Assault causing reasonable apprehension of grievous hurt
3. Assault with intent to commit rape
4. Assault with intent to kidnap
5. Assault with intent to wrongfully confine
6. Assault by acid attack (added by 2013 amendment)

**Right of private defence of PROPERTY (S.97/103 IPC) extends to causing death for:**
1. Robbery
2. House-breaking by night
3. Mischief by fire to dwelling house
4. Theft/mischief causing reasonable apprehension of death

**Limitations (S.99 IPC):**
- No right against public servant acting in good faith
- No right when there is time to seek public authorities' protection
- Right extends only to the harm necessary to repel the aggression

**Key principles:**
- Person must be under reasonable apprehension (objective test)
- Right is defensive, not punitive
- Cannot be exercised by aggressor

**Key cases:**
- *Darshan Singh v State of Punjab (2010)* — Detailed SC guidelines on S.100
- *Sekar v State (2002)* — Reasonable apprehension standard explained
pun: Complete defence if within limits — no punishment

## S.34 & S.149 IPC — Common Intention and Common Object

**S.34 — Common Intention:**
When a criminal act is done by several persons in furtherance of the common intention of all, each of such persons is liable for that act as if it were done by him alone.

**Essentials of S.34:**
1. Criminal act done by several persons (2 or more)
2. Done in furtherance of common intention
3. Participation in the criminal act (need not do the actual act)

**S.149 — Common Object (Unlawful Assembly):**
Every member of unlawful assembly is guilty of the offence committed in prosecution of the common object (or one that members knew was likely to be committed).

**Key distinction:**
| Feature | S.34 (Common Intention) | S.149 (Common Object) |
|---|---|---|
| No. of persons | 2 or more | 5 or more (unlawful assembly) |
| Prior meeting of minds | Required | Not necessarily required |
| Nature | Joint liability | Vicarious liability |
| Proof of participation | Necessary | Membership of assembly sufficient |

**Case laws:**
- *Barendra Kumar Ghosh v Emperor* — S.34 applies even to person standing guard outside
- *Lallan Rai v State of Bihar* — Common intention can form on the spot

## Section 406 IPC / Section 316 BNS — Criminal Breach of Trust

**Essentials:**
1. The accused was entrusted with property or with dominion over property
2. The accused dishonestly misappropriated, converted, used, or disposed of that property
3. OR dishonestly allowed any other person to do so
4. In violation of any direction of law or contract

**Punishment:** Up to 3 years or Fine or both (Bailable offence)

**Aggravated forms:**
- S.407 IPC: CBT by carrier/wharfinger/warehouse keeper — up to 7 years
- S.408 IPC: CBT by clerk/servant — up to 7 years
- S.409 IPC: CBT by public servant/banker/merchant/factor — Life or 10 years + Fine

**Key distinction from theft:**
- CBT: Property legitimately in accused's possession, later dishonestly dealt with
- Theft: Property taken WITHOUT consent/authority

**Case laws:**
- *Velji Raghavji Patel v State of Maharashtra* — Entrustment essential; mere possession insufficient
- *Superintendent & Remembrancer v Anil Kumar Bose* — CBT by company director discussed
pun: Up to 3 years or Fine or both

## Sudden and Grave Provocation — Exception 1 to S.300 IPC

**When culpable homicide reduces from murder to S.304:**
Exception 1 to S.300: When the act is done in the heat of passion upon a sudden and grave provocation AND the offender, by the provocation, is deprived of the power of self-control.

**Requirements:**
1. Provocation must be SUDDEN (not premeditated response)
2. Provocation must be GRAVE (serious enough to cause loss of self-control)
3. Act done before there was time to cool down
4. Provocation was not sought or voluntarily provoked by accused

**Cannot be pleaded when:**
- Provocation given by anything done in obedience of law or by public servant
- Provocation was by a lawful exercise of right of private defence by another
- Accused had time to cool down before committing the act

**Practical application:**
- Husband finding wife in adultery and killing in heat of passion — Exception 1 may apply
- Pre-planned killing after quarrel — Exception 1 does NOT apply
- Time gap between provocation and killing fatal to the defence

**Case laws:**
- *K.M. Nanavati v State of Maharashtra* — Famous adultery-provocation case; courts held provocation insufficient
- *Pulicherla Nagaraju v State of AP* — Guidelines for applying exception 1
pun: S.304 Part I: Life or 10 yrs; Part II: 10 yrs or fine

## Kidnapping and Abduction — Sections 363–374 IPC

**S.359 IPC — Two kinds of kidnapping:**
1. **Kidnapping from India (S.360):** Conveying any person beyond India without consent
2. **Kidnapping from lawful guardianship (S.361):** Taking a minor (below 16 male/18 female) or unsound person out of keeping of lawful guardian WITHOUT guardian's consent

**S.363 IPC:** Punishment for kidnapping — up to 7 years + Fine

**Aggravated forms:**
- S.364: Kidnapping to murder — Life or 10 years RI
- S.364A: Kidnapping for ransom/murder — Death or Life RI + Fine
- S.366: Kidnapping/abducting woman to compel marriage — up to 10 years
- S.366A/B: Procurement of minor girl for illicit intercourse
- S.367: Kidnapping to subject to grievous hurt/slavery
- S.374: Unlawful compulsory labour

**Abduction (S.362 IPC):** Compelling/inducing a PERSON (any age) by force/deceit to go from any place. Not an offence by itself — must be with specific intent.

**Key difference:**
| | Kidnapping | Abduction |
|---|---|---|
| Who | Minor/unsound | Any person |
| Means | Any means | Force/deceit |
| Intent | Intent irrelevant | Intent essential |
| Offence itself | Yes (S.363) | No — intent decides |

**Case laws:**
- *State of Haryana v Raja Ram* — Minor's consent irrelevant in kidnapping from guardianship

## Property Offences — Theft, Robbery, Dacoity

**Hierarchy of property offences:**

**THEFT (S.379 IPC / S.303 BNS):**
- Essentials: Dishonest intention + moveable property + out of possession of another + without consent + moving
- Punishment: Up to 3 years or Fine or both
- Bailable, Cognizable

**EXTORTION (S.383 IPC / S.308 BNS):**
- Intentionally putting person in fear of injury + dishonestly inducing delivery of property
- Punishment: Up to 3 years + Fine (S.384)
- Non-bailable, Cognizable

**ROBBERY (S.390 IPC / S.309 BNS):**
- Theft becomes robbery when force/fear of force used in committing theft, or carrying away stolen property
- Assault becomes robbery when force/fear used for extortion
- Punishment: RI up to 10 years + Fine (S.392); On highway: up to 14 years
- Non-bailable, Cognizable, Sessions Court

**DACOITY (S.394 IPC / S.310 BNS):**
- 5 or more persons conjointly committing or attempting robbery
- Punishment: Life imprisonment OR RI up to 10 years + Fine (S.395)
- Dacoity with murder (S.396): Death / Life / RI 10 yrs
- Non-bailable, Cognizable, Sessions Court

**Comparison table:**
| Offence | Persons | Force | Punishment |
|---|---|---|---|
| Theft | 1+ | No | 3 years |
| Extortion | 1+ | Fear | 3 years |
| Robbery | 1+ | Yes | 10 years |
| Dacoity | 5+ | Yes | Life |

## Indian Contract Act 1872 — Complete Law of Contract

**Section 10 — Essentials of a Valid Contract (all 6 must exist):**

1. **Offer and Acceptance (S.2(a)-(b)):** Definite offer + unconditional acceptance. Counter-offer kills original offer.
2. **Free Consent (S.13-22):** Must be free from coercion (S.15), undue influence (S.16), fraud (S.17), misrepresentation (S.18), mistake (S.20-22)
3. **Competency (S.11):** Must be (a) Major (18+), (b) Sound mind, (c) Not disqualified by law. Minors' contracts are VOID ab initio.
4. **Lawful Consideration (S.2(d), S.23):** 'Quid pro quo' — must exist, be real, and be lawful. Past consideration valid in India (unlike English law).
5. **Lawful Object (S.23):** Purpose must not be illegal, fraudulent, cause harm to others, or be opposed to public policy.
6. **Not Expressly Declared Void (S.26-30):** Agreements in restraint of marriage (S.26), trade (S.27), legal proceedings (S.28) are void.

**Types of contracts:**
- **Void (S.2(g)):** No legal effect from inception (minor's contract)
- **Voidable (S.2(i)):** Valid unless rescinded by the aggrieved party
- **Illegal:** Void + connected agreements also void
- **Unenforceable:** Valid but cannot be enforced (e.g., time-barred)

**Termination/Discharge of contract:**
- By performance (S.37-67)
- By agreement (S.62)
- By frustration/impossibility (S.56) — *Taylor v Caldwell* principle
- By breach (S.39)

**Remedies for breach (S.73-75):**
- Damages: Ordinary + Special (Hadley v Baxendale rule)
- Specific performance (SRA 1963)
- Injunction
- Quantum meruit (S.70)
- Rescission (S.64)

## Sections 73-74 ICA — Damages for Breach of Contract

**Section 73 — Compensation for Breach:**
Party who suffers breach entitled to receive compensation for:
1. Any loss or damage which naturally arose in the usual course of things from such breach, OR
2. Which the parties knew, when they made the contract, to be likely to result from a breach

**Hadley v Baxendale Rule (adopted by Indian courts):**
- Limb 1: Losses arising naturally from the breach (general damages)
- Limb 2: Losses in reasonable contemplation of both parties at time of contracting (special damages)

**Duty to mitigate:** Aggrieved party MUST take all reasonable steps to minimise their loss. Cannot recover damages for loss that could have been avoided by reasonable effort.

**Section 74 — Liquidated Damages and Penalty:**
When sum named in contract as payable on breach, court shall award REASONABLE COMPENSATION not exceeding that sum — regardless of whether actual damage/loss proved.

*Key change from English law: Indian law does not distinguish between 'liquidated damages' and 'penalty' — both treated equally and capped at reasonable compensation.*

**Types of damages:**
| Type | Description | When available |
|---|---|---|
| Ordinary/General | Natural consequence of breach | Always |
| Special/Consequential | Communicated special circumstances | If known to both parties |
| Nominal | Technical breach, no actual loss | Breach proven but no loss |
| Liquidated | Pre-agreed sum | S.74 — reasonable compensation |
| Exemplary | Not available in Indian contract law | N/A |

**Case laws:**
- *BSNL v Reliance Communications* — Liquidated damages in telecom contracts
- *Fateh Chand v Balkishan Das* — S.74 applies to all penalty/earnest money clauses

## Section 56 ICA — Doctrine of Frustration / Subsequent Impossibility

**Section 56 — Agreement to do impossible act is void. Also:**
A contract to do an act which, after the contract is made, becomes impossible or, by reason of some event which the promisor could not prevent, unlawful, shall become VOID when the act becomes impossible or unlawful.

**When frustration applies:**
1. There was a valid contract
2. After the contract, some event occurred which the promisor did not cause
3. The event made performance impossible or radically different from what was undertaken
4. The event was not foreseen/foreseeable by the parties

**Categories of frustrating events:**
- Physical destruction of subject matter (*Taylor v Caldwell*)
- Death/incapacity of a key person (personal service contracts)
- Supervening illegality
- Occurrence of foundation event (*Krell v Henry* — Coronation cases)
- Change in law
- Government action/requisition

**Force Majeure vs. Frustration:**
- Force majeure: Contractual clause covering specific events (must be in contract)
- Frustration: Statutory doctrine applying even without FM clause

**Effect of frustration:** Contract becomes VOID. Money paid is recoverable (S.65 ICA).

**COVID-19 Judicial guidance:**
- *Standard Retail Pvt Ltd v GS Global Corp (Bombay HC 2020)* — COVID lockdown alone not enough for frustration in commodity contracts
- Courts applied strict test: frustration requires impossibility, not mere commercial hardship

**Case laws:**
- *Satyabrata Ghose v Mugneeram Bangur (1954)* — Leading Indian case on frustration
limitation: 3 years from when contract becomes void

## Order 39, CPC 1908 — Temporary Injunction

**Three conditions for grant (all three must be satisfied):**
1. **Prima facie case:** Plaintiff must show a strong prima facie case in their favour — not a conclusive proof, but a triable question
2. **Balance of convenience:** The balance of convenience must be in favour of granting the injunction (more harm from non-granting than from granting)
3. **Irreparable injury:** The plaintiff would suffer irreparable injury if injunction is not granted (injury that cannot be compensated in money)

**Types of injunctions:**
- **Temporary/Interlocutory (O.39 R.1-2):** During pendency of suit
- **Ad-interim (O.39 R.3):** Without notice to opposite party in urgent cases — for 30 days initially
- **Permanent (S.37-42 SRA):** Final decree in the suit

**Procedure:**
1. Application under O.39 R.1 or R.2
2. Court may grant ex-parte ad-interim injunction (O.39 R.3)
3. Notice to opposite party → hearing → decision
4. Can be vacated on application by opposite party

**Undertaking as to damages:** Court can require plaintiff to give undertaking to compensate defendant if injunction turns out to be wrongly granted.

**Case laws:**
- *Dalpat Kumar v Prahlad Singh (1992)* — Three conditions restated by SC
- *Wander Ltd v Antox India Pvt Ltd (1990)* — Appellate court interference in injunction orders

## Writs Under Articles 32 & 226 — Complete Guide

**Five Writs:**

**1. HABEAS CORPUS ('To have the body'):**
- Purpose: Release of person illegally detained
- Lies against: State AND private persons
- Cannot be suspended except during National Emergency (Art.359)
- Available: Even if detention is under an Act of Parliament
- *Key case: ADM Jabalpur v Shivkant Shukla (Emergency case); DK Basu guidelines*

**2. MANDAMUS ('We command'):**
- Purpose: Command public authority to perform legal duty it has wrongly refused/failed to perform
- Lies against: Public bodies, corporations, inferior courts (NOT private individuals for private duties)
- Cannot issue: To President/Governor (Art.361 immunity), to Lok Sabha/RS Speaker (constitutional functions)
- *Key case: Rashid Ahmed v Municipal Board (1950)*

**3. CERTIORARI ('To be certified'):**
- Purpose: Quash the order of inferior court/tribunal/quasi-judicial body
- Grounds: Lack of jurisdiction, excess of jurisdiction, error of law apparent on face of record, violation of natural justice
- Lies against: Judicial/quasi-judicial bodies (not administrative)
- *Key case: T.C. Basappa v T. Nagappa*

**4. PROHIBITION:**
- Purpose: PREVENT inferior court from exceeding/usurping jurisdiction (issued before decision)
- Distinguished from Certiorari: Certiorari is post-decision; Prohibition is pre-decision
- Lies against: Only judicial/quasi-judicial bodies

**5. QUO WARRANTO ('By what authority'):**
- Purpose: Inquire into legality of person's claim to hold a public office
- Who can file: Any person (not just aggrieved party) — it is a public interest writ
- Lies against: Substantive public office created by law

**Art.226 vs. Art.32:**
| Feature | Art.226 | Art.32 |
|---|---|---|
| Court | High Court | Supreme Court |
| Scope | FRs + any other purpose | Only FRs |
| Territorial | Within HC jurisdiction | Pan-India |
| Discretionary? | Yes (alternate remedy bar) | Restricted discretion (FR case) |
| SLP from HC order | Yes (to SC under Art.136) | — |

## Complete Divorce Law in India

**A. HINDU MARRIAGE ACT 1955 — Section 13:**

**Grounds for divorce (either party):**
1. Adultery — sexual intercourse with person other than spouse after marriage
2. Cruelty — physical/mental causing reasonable apprehension of harm
3. Desertion — without reasonable cause for continuous period of ≥2 years
4. Conversion — to another religion
5. Unsound mind — incurably of unsound mind for ≥3 years
6. Venereal disease — in communicable form
7. Renunciation — entered holy order
8. Presumption of death — not heard of for ≥7 years

**Additional grounds for WIFE only (S.13(2)):**
- Husband had wife living at time of marriage (bigamy)
- Husband convicted of rape/sodomy/bestiality
- Non-resumption of cohabitation after maintenance order
- Marriage solemnized before 15 years

**Mutual Consent Divorce (S.13B HMA):**
- Conditions: Separated ≥1 year + unable to live together + both consent
- Procedure: Joint petition → First motion → 6-month cooling period (waivable) → Second motion → Decree
- *Amardeep Singh v Harbheen Kaur (2017)* — Cooling period waivable if all issues settled

**B. MUSLIM DIVORCE:**
- **Talaq-e-Ahsan:** Single pronouncement in a tuhr (clean period) + 3 months iddat — VALID
- **Talaq-e-Hasan:** Three pronouncements in three successive tuhrs — VALID
- **Triple Talaq (Talaq-ul-biddat):** VOID and illegal (Triple Talaq Act 2019) — imprisonment up to 3 years
- **Khula:** Wife-initiated divorce with return of mahr — needs husband's consent
- **Mubarat:** Mutual dissolution
- **Judicial divorce:** Under Dissolution of Muslim Marriages Act 1939

**C. SPECIAL MARRIAGE ACT 1954:**
- For inter-religion marriages and civil marriages
- S.27: Divorce grounds (similar to HMA)
- S.28: Mutual consent divorce
- Marriage registered with Marriage Registrar

**D. CHRISTIAN DIVORCE:**
- Indian Divorce Act 1869
- Grounds: Adultery (+ cruelty or desertion for husband's petition); adultery alone for wife
- Amended 2001 to include cruelty and desertion as separate grounds

## Maintenance Law in India — Complete Guide

**A. Section 125 CrPC / Section 144 BNSS 2023 — Criminal Court Maintenance:**

**Who can claim:**
1. Wife (including divorced wife — until remarriage)
2. Minor children (legitimate/illegitimate)
3. Adult children (if unable to maintain themselves due to physical/mental abnormality)
4. Father/Mother unable to maintain themselves

**Against whom:** Person having sufficient means who neglects/refuses to maintain

**Jurisdiction:** Magistrate of First Class (JMFC)

**Quantum:** No upper limit — based on income and need (courts typically award ₹3,000 to ₹30,000+ depending on income)

**Limitation:** Application can be made at any time while the entitlement exists

**B. Section 24 HMA 1955 — Maintenance Pendente Lite:**
- During pendency of matrimonial proceedings
- Either spouse can claim
- Norm: 20-25% of respondent's net income
- Includes litigation expenses
- *Jasbir Kaur Sehgal* — 25% norm established

**C. Section 25 HMA 1955 — Permanent Alimony and Maintenance:**
- After decree of divorce/judicial separation/restitution
- Court grants gross sum or monthly/periodical amount
- Ceases on remarriage of recipient or court modification
- Can be varied by court on change in circumstances

**D. Muslim Women — Post-Divorce Maintenance:**
- *Shah Bano case (1985)*: Muslim women entitled to S.125 CrPC maintenance
- Muslim Women (Protection of Rights on Divorce) Act 1986: Reasonable provision + maintenance during iddat period only
- *Danial Latifi v UOI (2001)*: Entire maintenance for post-divorce life must be paid during iddat period
- S.125 CrPC also available (*Shabana Bano v Imran Khan 2009*)

**E. Maintenance for Children (Divorced parents):**
- Either parent can be directed to pay for minor children
- Court considers: welfare of child, income of both parents, standard of living
- *Nil Ratan Kundu v Abhijit Kundu* — SC guidelines on child maintenance

## Hindu Succession Act 1956 (amended 2005) — Complete Guide

**Two types of property:**
1. **Ancestral/Coparcenary Property:** Inherited from father/paternal grandfather/great-grandfather. HUF members have birthright.
2. **Self-Acquired Property:** Earned by individual — can give/will to anyone.

**S.6 — Daughters as Coparceners (2005 Amendment):**
- Daughters are coparceners by birth (same as sons)
- Same rights and liabilities as sons
- Can demand partition
- *Vineeta Sharma v Rakesh Sharma (SC 2020)*: Applies even if father died before 9.9.2005

**Intestate Succession — Class I Heirs (Schedule):**
Son, Daughter, Widow, Mother, Son of a pre-deceased son, Daughter of a pre-deceased son, etc.
ALL Class I heirs take simultaneously and equally.

**Class II Heirs:** Father, siblings — take only if no Class I heir.

**S.15 — Succession of a Hindu Female's Property:**
1. First to sons, daughters, husband
2. Then to heirs of husband
3. Then to mother and father
4. Then to heirs of father
5. Then to heirs of mother

**Testamentary succession (Wills):**
- Hindu can make will for self-acquired property AND their share of coparcenary property
- Will must comply with Indian Succession Act 1925 (registration optional but advisable)
- Attestation by two witnesses required
- Probate mandatory in Presidency towns

**Partition of HUF:**
- Any coparcener (including daughter post-2005) can demand partition
- Once demanded, partition is a matter of right
- Partial partition possible (by property or by parties)
- Partition deed should be registered

**Key cases:**
- *Vineeta Sharma v Rakesh Sharma (2020)* — Daughters' rights retrospective
- *Prakash v Phulwati (2016)* — overruled by Vineeta Sharma on retrospectivity

## Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code 2016 — Complete Framework

**Objective:** To consolidate all insolvency laws, maximize value of assets, promote entrepreneurship, availability of credit, and balance interests of all stakeholders.

**Three types of CIRP applications:**

**S.7 — Financial Creditor (FC):**
- FC = Bank, NBFC, bond/debenture holder
- Default threshold: ₹1 Crore
- Must file: Evidence of debt + default
- NCLT decision: Within 14 days

- Same ₹1 Crore threshold

- Day 1: Admission → Moratorium takes effect (S.14)
- Day 1: IRP (Interim Resolution Professional) appointed
- Day 30: IRP submits information memorandum
- Day 30: Committee of Creditors (CoC) constituted
- Day 30-180: CIRP period
- Day 180: Resolution plan or extension to 270/330 days
- Day 270+: LIQUIDATION if no plan

**Moratorium (S.14):**
All judicial proceedings, SARFAESI, DRT, execution proceedings against corporate debtor STAYED.

**Resolution Plan must:**
- Maximize value of assets
- Provide for payment to operational creditors ≥ liquidation value
- Comply with applicable laws
- Be approved by ≥66% voting share of CoC

**Key cases:**
- *Innoventive Industries v ICICI Bank (2017)* — IBC overrides all other laws
- *Swiss Ribbons v UOI (2019)* — Constitutional validity of IBC upheld

## Key Employee Benefit Laws in India

**A. Employees' Provident Fund (EPF) Act 1952:**

**Applicability:** Establishments with 20+ employees (several industries notified with lower threshold)

**Contribution rates:**
- Employee contribution: 12% of basic salary + DA
- Employer contribution: 12% (3.67% to EPF + 8.33% to EPS)

**Interest:** Currently ~8.15% p.a. (notified annually)

**Withdrawal:**
- Full withdrawal on retirement (58 years) or unemployment for 2+ months
- Partial withdrawal allowed for house purchase, medical treatment, marriage, education

**Penalty for non-compliance:** Criminal prosecution — up to 1 year imprisonment + fine. Damages up to 100% of arrears.

**B. Employees' State Insurance (ESI) Act 1948:**

**Applicability:** Factories/establishments with 10+ employees; wages ≤ ₹21,000/month (₹25,000 for disabled persons)

**Contribution:**
- Employee: 0.75% of wages
- Employer: 3.25% of wages

**Benefits:** Medical, sickness (70% of wages for 91 days), maternity (100% wages for 26 weeks), disablement, dependant benefit, funeral expenses

**C. Payment of Gratuity Act 1972:**

**Applicability:** Establishments with 10+ employees

**Eligibility:** Completed **5 years** of continuous service (4 years 240 days for seasonal workers)

**Calculation:** 15 days' wages × number of completed years of service ÷ 26

**Maximum:** ₹20 lakh (enhanced in 2018)

**When payable:** Retirement, resignation after 5 years, death (to nominee), disablement

**Forfeiture:** Allowed only for wilful omission, negligence causing damage, or offences involving moral turpitude

**Limitation for claim:** 30 days from date it becomes payable

## Transfer of Property Act 1882 — Complete Guide

**A. SALE (S.54 TPA):**
Transfer of ownership in exchange for price paid/promised/partly paid.
- Immovable property >₹100: Must be by registered instrument
- Sale deed + stamp duty + registration = valid transfer
- *Suraj Lamp Industries v State of Haryana* — GPA sales invalid; registered deed mandatory

**Six types of mortgages:**

|---|---|---|
| Simple Mortgage | Personal liability + no possession | |
| Mortgage by Conditional Sale | Becomes sale on default | |
| Usufructuary Mortgage | Mortgagee takes possession + rents | |
| English Mortgage | Absolute transfer + reconveyance on repayment | |
| Mortgage by Deposit of Title Deeds (Equitable) | Deposit of title deeds only | In notified cities only |
| Anomalous | Any other type | |

Transfer of right to enjoy immovable property for a certain time in consideration of price/premium/rent.

- Determination of lease: Forfeiture, notice to quit, efflux of time

**D. GIFT (S.122 TPA):**
Transfer of existing moveable/immovable property voluntarily, without consideration.

- Immovable property gift: Must be registered

- Onerous gift (S.127): Donee can reject the entire gift

**E. ADVERSE POSSESSION (S.28 Limitation Act + Article 65):**
Acquiring ownership of another's property by continuous, open, hostile, exclusive possession for 12 years.
- Possession must be: actual, continuous, open (not concealed), hostile (adverse to title)
- Period: 12 years for private land; 30 years for government land
- *Hemaji Waghaji Jat v Bhikhabhai Khengarbhai Harijan* — Constitutional validity of adverse possession confirmed

## Indian Evidence Act 1872 / Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam 2023 — Complete Guide

**Structure of IEA:** 3 Parts — Relevancy (S.1-55), Proof (S.56-100), Production & Effect of Evidence (S.101-167)

**Burden of Proof (S.101-114):**
- S.101: Burden of proof on party who asserts the affirmative
- S.102: Burden shifts in civil cases — on party who will fail if no evidence given
- S.103: Burden of proving particular fact on person who wishes court to believe it
- S.105: Burden on accused to prove exceptions (insanity, self-defence)

**Relevancy vs. Admissibility:**
- Relevant: Facts logically connected to the issue (S.5-55)
- Admissible: Facts that can actually be placed before the court (may be relevant but excluded by law — e.g., privileged communications)

**CONFESSION (S.24-30):**
- S.24: Confession caused by inducement/threat/promise from person in authority = irrelevant
- S.25: Confession to police officer = NOT admissible (absolutely excluded)
- S.26: Confession in police custody = NOT admissible (unless before Magistrate)
- S.27: EXCEPTION — So much of confession as directly leads to discovery of fact = admissible
- S.30: Confession of one co-accused against another — can be taken into account but needs corroboration

**DYING DECLARATION (S.32(1)):**
- Statement by a person who is dead/cannot be found/is incapable, as to cause of their death
- No oath/cross-examination requirement
- Can be sole basis for conviction if found reliable (*Khushal Rao v State of Bombay*)
- Must be complete and consistent; suspicious circumstances require corroboration

**FIR:**
- S.154 CrPC/S.173 BNSS: First Information Report
- Not substantive evidence — can only be used to corroborate/contradict the maker
- *Lalita Kumari v Govt of UP (2014)* — Police must mandatorily register FIR for cognizable offence

**EXPERT OPINION (S.45-51):**
- Courts may take opinion of expert in: foreign law, science, art, handwriting, finger impressions
- Expert opinion is only an opinion — not conclusive; can be rejected

**ELECTRONIC EVIDENCE (S.65A-65B IEA / S.63 BSA 2023):**
- S.65B IEA: Electronic record admissible only with certificate from responsible person
- *Arjun Panditrao Khotkar v Kailash Kushanrao Goratyal (2020)* — S.65B certificate mandatory; original device need not be produced
- BSA 2023: S.63 streamlines electronic evidence admissibility

**Presumptions (S.112-114):**
- S.112: Child born during valid marriage = legitimate (conclusive)
- S.113B: Dowry death presumption (rebuttable)
- S.114: Court may presume existence of facts it deems probable

'Safe harbour' protection — intermediaries not liable for third-party content if:
- They don't initiate transmission
- Don't select receiver
- Don't modify content
- Comply with due diligence guidelines (IT Intermediary Rules 2021)

**How to report cybercrime:**
- National Cybercrime Reporting Portal: cybercrime.gov.in
- Helpline: 1930
- Nearest cyber cell of police

## Online Defamation and Social Media Law in India

**Defamation under IPC (S.499-500):**
**Definition (S.499):** Making or publishing an imputation about a person intending to harm or knowing/having reason to believe it will harm their reputation.

**Forms:** Written (libel), Spoken (slander) — both covered under S.499 IPC

**Essentials:**
1. Making or publishing an imputation about a person
2. Such imputation must have been made by words/signs/visible representations
3. The imputation must be false
4. The person making the imputation must know/have reason to believe it would harm reputation

**Punishment (S.500):** Up to 2 years imprisonment or Fine or both. **Non-cognizable, Bailable, Compoundable.**

**Exceptions to defamation (S.499 — 10 exceptions):**
- Truth for public good
- Fair comment on public conduct of public servants
- Fair report of court proceedings
- Publication of official reports
- Merits of public case
- Opinion on author/artist's work
- Censure in good faith by person having authority
- Accusation to authorised person
- Imputation made in good faith for protection of interest
- Caution in good faith

**Online Defamation specifics:**
- Social media posts, comments, tweets, WhatsApp forwards — all covered
- S.66A IT Act (offensive messages) was STRUCK DOWN — cannot be used
- Use: S.499/500 IPC + IT Act S.66 (if involves hacking/fake accounts)
- Jurisdiction: Where victim resides OR where defamatory content was uploaded

**Civil remedy:**
- Suit for damages in civil court
- Injunction to remove content
- No criminal record needed

**Filing complaint:**
- Police complaint (though non-cognizable — Magistrate may direct police to investigate)
- Or file private complaint directly before Magistrate under S.190(1)(a) CrPC

## Bail Law in India — Complete Guide (CrPC + BNSS 2023)

**Types of Bail:**

**1. BAIL IN BAILABLE OFFENCES (S.436 CrPC / S.478 BNSS):**
- Accused has RIGHT to bail — cannot be refused
- Police/court MUST release on bail
- Can be released on personal bond (without surety)
- No conditions can be imposed

**2. BAIL IN NON-BAILABLE OFFENCES (S.437 CrPC / S.480 BNSS):**
- Discretionary — court weighs:
  - Gravity of offence
  - Prima facie guilt
  - Criminal antecedents
  - Flight risk
  - Likelihood of repeating offence
  - Threat to witnesses
- Cannot be granted by police (only court)
- Must not be granted if offence punishable with death/life imprisonment (unless woman, child under 16, sick/infirm person)
- BNSS 2023 new provision: Person in custody for 1/2 of maximum imprisonment for offence = entitled to bail (default bail for undertrial reform)

**3. ANTICIPATORY BAIL (S.438 CrPC / S.482 BNSS):**
- Before arrest — in anticipation
- Sessions Court or High Court
- Conditions can be attached
- After *Sushila Aggarwal (2020)*: Can continue till end of trial

**4. DEFAULT BAIL / STATUTORY BAIL (S.167(2) CrPC / S.187(3) BNSS):**
- If police fail to file charge sheet within:
  - 60 days (for offences punishable with death/life/≥10 years)
  - 90 days (for other offences)
- Accused entitled to bail as of RIGHT — called 'indefeasible right'
- *Uday Mohanlal Acharya v State of Maharashtra (2001)* — Right accrues on expiry of period

**5. BAIL BY SESSIONS COURT/HC (S.439 CrPC / S.483 BNSS):**
- Sessions Court and HC have special powers
- Can grant bail even if Magistrate refused
- Can impose additional/varied conditions

**Standard bail conditions:**
- Not to leave country without permission
- Report to police station on specified dates
- Surrender passport
- Not to tamper with evidence or threaten witnesses
- Provide surety (person who guarantees accused's appearance)

**Cancellation of bail (S.437(5), S.439(2)):**
- On violation of conditions
- On discovery of new material
- On evidence of tampering/fleeing

## FIR (First Information Report) — Complete Law

**What is an FIR?** The information of a cognizable offence given to police, which sets the criminal law in motion.

**Legal provision:** S.154 CrPC / S.173 BNSS 2023

**Mandatory registration:**
*Lalita Kumari v Govt of UP (2014 SC 5-judge bench):* Registration of FIR is MANDATORY for cognizable offences. Police cannot conduct preliminary inquiry before registering FIR in cognizable offences.

**Zero FIR:**
FIR can be registered at ANY police station regardless of jurisdiction. Transferred to appropriate station after registration. Critical in urgent cases.

**Procedure (S.154 CrPC):**
1. Informant gives information to officer in charge
2. Must be written down and read to informant
3. Signed by informant
4. Copy to informant FREE of cost (S.154(2))
5. Entered in daily diary/station house register

**If police refuse to register FIR:**
- S.154(3): Informant can send substance by post to Superintendent of Police
- S.156(3): Magistrate can order police to register FIR
- Writ petition (Mandamus) in High Court
- Private complaint before Magistrate (S.190 CrPC)

**Legal value of FIR:**
- NOT substantive evidence — only FIR maker's prior statement
- Can be used to corroborate or contradict maker (S.157 IEA)
- Can be used to show first statement made promptly
- Delay in filing FIR — creates suspicion (must be explained)

**Chargesheet (S.173 CrPC / S.193 BNSS):**
- Police report filed after investigation
- Must be filed within: 60 days (serious offences) or 90 days (others)
- Failure = default bail (S.167(2))

**Key cases:**
- *Lalita Kumari v Govt of UP* — Mandatory FIR registration
- *State of Haryana v Bhajan Lal* — Quashing of FIR — when HC can interfere

## Section 482 CrPC / Section 528 BNSS — Inherent Powers of High Court

**Provision:** 'Nothing in this Code shall be deemed to limit or affect the inherent powers of the High Court to make such orders as may be necessary to give effect to any order under this Code, or to prevent abuse of the process of any court or otherwise to secure the ends of justice.'

**Three purposes of S.482:**
1. To give effect to an order under CrPC
2. To prevent abuse of the process of any court
3. To otherwise secure the ends of justice

**Most common use — Quashing of FIR/Complaint:**
HC can quash when:
- No cognizable offence made out on face of FIR
- Allegations are absurd, inherently improbable, or cannot constitute the offence
- Criminal proceeding is manifestly attended with mala fide
- Dispute is purely civil in nature but dressed as criminal case
- Compounding between parties (in compoundable offences)

***Bhajan Lal* Categories (State of Haryana v Bhajan Lal 1992):**
7 categories where HC should quash under S.482:
1. Allegations do not constitute any offence
2. Allegations patently absurd and inherently improbable
3. Uncontroverted allegations do not disclose essential elements
4. Complaint not filed by authorised person
5. FIR discloses only civil dispute
6. Legal bar to prosecution exists
7. Criminal proceedings manifestly mala fide

**Cannot quash:**
- When disputed facts need trial
- When offence is serious (murder, rape) — court must be very slow
- On mere denial by accused

**Limitation:** No limitation period for S.482 petition — but laches considered

## FEMA 1999 + PMLA 2002 — Foreign Exchange & Money Laundering

**A. Foreign Exchange Management Act 1999 (FEMA):**

**Nature:** Civil law (replaced FERA 1973 which was criminal). Violations = civil penalties, not imprisonment (except in some cases).

**Regulation structure:**
- RBI regulates capital account transactions
- Current account transactions broadly permitted
- Schedule I: Prohibited transactions
- Schedule II-III: RBI/Govt. permission required

**Key violations:**
- Holding foreign currency above permitted limit
- Remitting money abroad without permission
- Investing in foreign companies without RBI approval
- Non-repatriation of export proceeds within specified time
- Hawala transactions

**Penalties under FEMA:**
- Civil penalty up to 3× the amount involved
- Adjudication by Enforcement Directorate (ED)
- Appeal to FEMA Appellate Tribunal → HC
- Repeated violation: Criminal prosecution possible

**B. Prevention of Money Laundering Act 2002 (PMLA):**

**Money laundering:** Process of making proceeds of crime appear legitimate.
Three stages: Placement → Layering → Integration

**Key provision — S.3:** Knowingly assisting/being party to process/activity connected with proceeds of crime = money laundering offence.

**Punishment:** 3 to 7 years RI (up to 10 years in narcotics-related cases) + Fine

**Powers of ED:**
- Attachment of property (provisional — 180 days)
- Arrest without warrant
- Search and seizure
- Summons for examination

**PMLA bail conditions (S.45):**
- Twin conditions: Court satisfied accused is NOT guilty + shall not commit another offence
- Very restrictive — bail difficult to get in PMLA cases
- *Vijay Madanlal Choudhary v UOI (2022)* — S.45 conditions upheld as constitutional

**Predicate offences:** Schedule to PMLA lists offences under IPC, NDPS, FEMA, Companies Act, etc. whose proceeds constitute money laundering if laundered.

## Section 197 CrPC / Section 218 BNSS — Sanction for Prosecution

**Provision:** When any person who is or was a Judge, Magistrate, or public servant not removable from office save by or with sanction of the Government — if accused of any offence alleged to have been committed while acting or purporting to act in discharge of official duty — no court shall take cognizance except with prior sanction of the appropriate government.

**When sanction is required:**
1. The person is or was a public servant
2. The alleged offence was committed while acting or purporting to act in discharge of official duty
3. The public servant belongs to a category not removable without government sanction

**Test for 'official duty':**
Not merely whether the act was done as a public servant, but whether the act was so integrally connected with official duty that it cannot be separated therefrom.

*Harihar Prasad v State of Bihar* — Sanction required only where offence is directly connected to official function; cannot be used as shield for private criminal acts.

**Who grants sanction:**
- Central Government: Central government employees
- State Government: State government employees

**Effect of no sanction:** Court takes cognizance without sanction = proceedings void from inception.

**Exception:** Does not protect acts done in personal capacity even if done during official hours.

**Key cases:**
- *State of Orissa v Ganesh Chandra Jew* — Sanction protects officers from frivolous prosecution
- *R. Balakrishna Pillai v State of Kerala* — Scope of 'discharge of official duty' explained

## POCSO Act 2012 — Protection of Children from Sexual Offences

**Key definitions:**
- 'Child' = person below 18 years
- Gender-neutral — protects both boys and girls

**Offences and Punishments:**
| Offence | Section | Minimum Punishment |
|---|---|---|
| Penetrative sexual assault | S.3 | 10 years RI |
| Aggravated penetrative sexual assault | S.5 | 20 years RI |
| (On child under 12 years) | S.5(m) | 20 yrs to Death |
| Sexual assault (non-penetrative) | S.7 | 3 years RI |
| Aggravated sexual assault | S.9 | 5 years RI |
| Sexual harassment of child | S.11 | 3 years |
| Using child for pornography | S.13 | 5 years |
| Abetment and attempt | S.17-18 | Same as offence |

**Presumption of guilt (S.29):** Court SHALL presume accused guilty UNLESS accused proves innocence. Reverse burden of proof.

**Special procedure:**
- Trial before Special Court (designated by State Govt.)
- Trial to be completed within 1 year (S.35)
- Trial in-camera — identity of child NOT to be disclosed
- Child Welfare Committee (CWC) to be informed
- Child to be examined only once; video-conferencing allowed
- No cross-examination of child about character/conduct

**Mandatory reporting (S.19):**
Any person including child who has knowledge of offence MUST report to Special Juvenile Police Unit or local police. Failure = imprisonment up to 6 months + fine.

**Intermediary (S.20):** Media/studio using internet must report knowledge of child pornography. Failure = imprisonment up to 1 year.
